A.biggest_strength: Exceptional visual explanation of the function call mechanism, featuring semantic color-coding, animated data chips that visually bind arguments to parameters and return values to caller expressions, real compiler bytecode/assembly listings, and an interactive empirical stack-limit benchmark.
A.biggest_weakness: The primary interactive step-through widget directly supports only 6 languages (Python, JavaScript, Ruby, C, Java, Rust), leaving the remaining languages to the reference table below.

B.biggest_strength: Broad interactive language coverage with 14 selectable language tabs (including C#, PHP, Swift, Go, Kotlin, Haskell, and x86-64 assembly), each with working code and dedicated architectural call/return cards.
B.biggest_weakness: The visual explanation of the function call mechanism is weak: stack frames are merely static text cards that appear and disappear without visualizing data flow, parameter binding, or return value substitution, and the page completely omits reduced-motion accessibility.
factual_errors: Subtitle claims '13 languages' but presents 14 tabs (13 high-level languages plus x86-64 assembly).

In Haskell, the step-by-step runner depicts arguments being evaluated eagerly before the call and sumOfSquares executing before print, which contradicts Haskell's actual non-strict/lazy call-by-need evaluation model (though noted in passing in the explanatory text).

structured_output.reasons: Page A is the clear overall winner because it actually visualizes how a function call works. Through synchronized animated chips, semantic color-coding, in-frame expression reduction, and live compiler/bytecode disassemblies, a reader can see the physical mechanics of argument binding, stack growth, and return value substitution. While Page B provides impressive language coverage with 14 interactive tabs and solid architectural notes, its visual presentation relies on basic text cards popping on and off, lacking true visual explanation and omitting reduced-motion accessibility.
